newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African leader sues for peace.
newsitem.headline: Central African leader sues for peace.

text.p: Central African Republic President Ange-Felix Patasse began contacts on Tuesday to end an army mutiny, saying he wanted to avoid bloodshed in the country.
The mutiny erupted on November 16 while Patasse was in Europe. The president returned on Tuesday and started working for an end to the impoverished country's third army revolt this year.
But officials said a planned meeting with his opponents had been put off to Wednesday. They gave no explanation.

French troops based in the former French colony under bilateral accords helped put down a more bloody revolt over pay and status in May. They have been guarding key points in Bangui since soldiers came out in a sequel to previous uprisings.

"My order is: I don't want a Rwanda here, I don't want a Burundi, I don't want a Liberia," Patasse said in a broadcast, referring to countries that have went through or are now undergoing bloody ethnic and power struggles.
He called for respect for the constitution, invoking the name of revered founding president Barthelemy Boganda.
"We would have betrayed Barthelemy Boganda a thousand times over if we plunged our country into clan, tribal and regional rifts," he said in the broadcast message on state television.
Church-brokered negotiations that began on Saturday broke off on Monday when government representatives failed to attend.
Patasse thanked French President Jacques Chirac for ordering troops at France's important African garrison in Bangui to intervene this time and in May and for support in April.
French troops in Central African Republic are backed by warplanes and have been pivotal to France's numerous interventions in its former African colonies, notably Chad.

The bases played a key role in a French military mission in Rwanda in 1994 to protect refugees at the height of civil war and massacres. They are expected to be important in any French deployment to help war refugees in eastern Zaire if the United Nations authorises a multinational force promoted by France.

Paris reinforced the Bangui base last week bringing the troop strength there to 1,500. But mutineers, who have demanded Patasse's dismissal, have warned the French not to use force to shore up the president.

"If France wants to use all its might to tame Central African Republic it can go ahead... But the day France uses such force is the day we will set Bangui on fire," rebel spokesman Sergeant Roger Kongbossomo told Reuters on Monday.
Speaking before Patasse's arrival, he said the president should never return to the country.

"The president has introduced tribalism in the administration and army," Kongbossomo said. "He has distributed arms to his militants and entered alliances with foreign forces to the detriment of the national army."
The mutineers have made no public comment since Patasse's return.
French troops using helicopter gunships and armoured vehicles fought bloody battles with rebel soldiers in May when the army mutiny was followed by devastating looting in Bangui.
This time the French appear to be avoiding any direct confrontation with rebels. Mutineers have gone about unhindered as they disarm members of a civilian militia loyal to Patasse.

The army is divided between soldiers from Patasse's northern region and militants from the south, suspected of allegiance to former president Andre Kolingba, one of several candidates defeated by Patasse in multiparty elections in 1993.
The mutineers have also demanded pay from 1992 and 1993 and for Patasse to revoke a decree ordering a regiment involved in the pay revolts in April and May to a base out of the capital.
